amendments.rule: In a construct chain, the English relational expression belongs to the nomen rectum, headed on that noun. This is normally *of*, handled exactly as a Greek genitive `of + noun`, but where the ASV recasts the construct relation with *from*, *for*, *in*, *to*, *over*, or another preposition, that expression belongs there too. The construct state of the first noun is what signals the relation, but the first noun's unit takes only its own English word. **The rectum may be a pronominal suffix rather than a noun, and nothing changes.** Where the ASV renders such a suffix not with a possessive but with *of* and a pronoun — `כֻּלָּם` → *all of them*, `מַרְבִּיתָם` → *the greatest part of them* — the whole *of + pronoun* is the suffix's one unit, headed on the pronoun under rule 24, and the construct noun keeps only its own word: `כֹּל` takes *all*, never *all of*. Do not read that *of* as part of an English quantifier or as licensed by the construct noun's own state, for the reason this rule's third sentence gives. The corpus aligns a suffix to *of them* headed on *them* in 116 units and records no `כֹּל` → *all of* treatment, and where the construct noun's own English is something else the division shows in a single unit: `כֻּלָּם` → *five of them in all* gives *in all* to `כֹּל` and *of them* to the suffix. Where the ASV writes a possessive or a bare pronoun instead, rule 18 governs as before and there is no *of* to place. **But the word the construct holds must be one the ASV has written as a noun, and a participle or infinitive it has written as an English verb is not one.** Where the ASV renders the governing word by an English verb phrase — a light verb with its complement under rule 44, or any verb reaching its own object — and writes the *of*, *unto* or other preposition that English verb needs to reach the suffix, the word answers to the verb's valency and not to a relation between two nominals: it joins the verb's unit under rule 44's supplied-preposition clause, headed where that rule heads it, and the suffix keeps only the pronoun rule 18 writes for it. `לְהַכִּירֵנִי` → *that thou shouldest take knowledge* ***of*** *me* and `מַכִּירֵךְ` → *he that did take knowledge* ***of*** *thee* divide alike, though the first is an infinitive construct and the second a participle in construct state, because the ASV wrote one idiom for both and the Hebrew wrote a bare object suffix in both. Decide it by the subtraction test this rule already runs: drop the English preposition and ask whether the relation between two nominals has gone, as it has in *all of them*, or whether an English verb has been left unable to reach its object, as it is in *take knowledge thee*. Rule 44 states the same boundary from its own side, and rule 33 states it again in deferring only to a governing verb the ASV has itself rendered as an English verb; what the morpheme is tagged is no part of the condition, and what the ASV made of it is the whole of it. **A quantifying construct noun with a nominal rectum is read on exactly those terms.** Where `כֹּל`, `אֶחָד` or another quantifier stands in construct on a noun and the ASV writes an *of* between the two, that *of* is the chain's own relation and belongs to the rectum, the quantifier keeping only the word written for it: `אַחַד שְׁעָרֶיךָ` → *any* … *of thy gates* and `כָּל־עֵץ` → *any kind of tree* give *of gates* and *of tree* to their recta. **A generic noun the ASV supplies to expand the quantifier does not move that *of*.** Such a noun joins the quantifier's own unit under rule 31, which heads it on the word carrying the lexeme, so `כֹּל` takes *any kind* headed on *any*, exactly as it takes a bare *any* under rule 15 where the ASV supplies nothing. Do not read *all of*, *any of* or *any kind of* as one indivisible English quantifier: the *of* stands between the two nouns the Hebrew writes, and the subtraction test rules 16 and 31 use finds the relation between them gone when it is dropped. A partitive `מִן` before the noun is not this case, since no construct relation stands there and no morpheme but the preposition licenses either word: `מִן־הַבָּשָׂר` → *any of the flesh* is one unit on the `מִן`, headed on *any* under rule 24. **But a preposition that renders the construct noun's own lexeme is that noun's rendering and not the relation's.** Where the first noun is itself a directional or relational word and the ASV spends its one English word on that lexeme instead of writing a noun for it — `דֶּרֶךְ הַצָּפוֹן` → *toward the north*, `דֶּרֶךְ הַקָּדִים` → *toward the east* — the preposition belongs to the construct noun and heads its unit, while the rectum takes only its own word and the rectum's article takes the written *the* under rule 29. Decide it by the subtraction test rules 16, 31 and 43 use: drop the English preposition and ask whether the construct noun has lost its whole rendering or only the relation between the two nouns has gone. Where the construct noun would be left with nothing at all, the word is its own and this rule's first sentence does not reach it; where the construct noun keeps an English word of its own — `דֶּרֶךְ אַמָּה אֶחָת` → *a way of one cubit* — the first sentence stands and the *of* goes to the rectum. Do not mark such a construct `unrepresented` in order to give its preposition to the rectum: that leaves a lexical noun holding a plain English rendering unaligned, against rule 2. The corpus renders a construct `דֶּרֶךְ` by *toward*, *is toward* or *was toward* in eighteen units, always headed on the preposition, and records no unit where the rectum of such a phrase holds the preposition while the construct goes unrepresented. Two riders. Where a Hebrew preposition stands before such a construct noun and the ASV writes a single English rendering for the pair, rule 30 fuses them instead, whether that rendering is one word, as `לִפְנֵי` → *before*, or a compound preposition written in two or three, as `לְעֻמַּת` → *answerable to*, which the corpus fuses at EZK.40.18 and EZK.48.13, 18 (twice) and 21 and nowhere splits. Read rule 30's condition here as one rendering rather than one token, exactly as that rule states it: a second English word defeats the condition only where the ASV spends it on one morpheme in particular, and subtracting the *to* of *answerable to* leaves no morpheme short of a rendering of its own, since the construct noun is not a word the ASV ever writes alone; and where the phrase is the predicate of a verbless clause the construction-supplied copula joins the construct noun's unit under rule 20, as `דֶּרֶךְ הַצָּפוֹן` → *were toward the north*. **And a second `דֶּרֶךְ` standing in the same phrase is not a repetition the ASV renders once.** `הַדֶּרֶךְ דֶּרֶךְ הַצָּפוֹן` → *the way toward the north* gives *the way* to the absolute, with its article taking the *the*, and *toward* to the construct, and rule 22 reaches neither, because each has an English word of its own.
amendments.why: Rule 19's suffix-rectum sentence reads as covering any *of + pronoun* the ASV writes after a construct word, which is what RUT.2.19 reached for in giving *of thee* to the object suffix of `מַכִּירֵךְ` while RUT.2.10 gave the identical *of* of *take knowledge of me* to the verb under rule 44. The two rules met in one chapter and the over-broad sentence won in one verse and lost in the other, so the qualification belongs in rule 19's own text rather than in a new rule pointing back at it. The added paragraph states the boundary, gives the chapter's minimal pair, and routes the decision through the subtraction test rule 19 already uses. It contradicts nothing: the corpus's 116 `of them` suffix units are nominal chains, which the paragraph leaves untouched, and rule 44's own sentence on an object suffix reached through a supplied preposition (`יִבְּמָהּ` → *perform the duty of a husband's brother unto her*) already says the same thing from the other side, as does rule 33's deferral clause.

conventions: `נָכַר` hiphil with a bare object suffix is rendered *take knowledge of X* at RUT.2.10 and RUT.2.19. In both the supplied *of* is the preposition the English light-verb phrase needs to reach that suffix and joins the verb's unit under rule 44, the suffix keeping only its pronoun and the unit heading on *knowledge*. Rule 19's *of + pronoun* suffix-rectum sentence governs a relation between two nominals, as `כֻּלָּם` → *all of them* is, and does not reach an *of* an English verb's valency licenses; the state MACULA tags the governing word in — infinitive construct at v.10, participle in construct state at v.19 — is not what decides it.

RUT.2.23 `עַד־כְּלוֹת קְצִיר־הַשְּׂעֹרִים` → *unto the end of barley harvest*: in a three-member chain carrying its only article on the innermost rectum, with a single written *the* standing before the outermost construct's own word, the chapter gives that *the* to the outer construct as a supplied determiner (rule 29) and marks both articles `unrepresented`, no determiner standing before either article's own word. Rule 29's fronting sentence, which would give the *the* to the first article, was read and set aside because the word determines a noun outside the sub-chain the article stands in and the outer construct independently calls for a supplied one; rule 29's multi-level sentence contemplates a second written *the* and there is none here. The reading is hedged and the competing one is named.

`הַיּוֹם` → *to day* is divided at RUT.2.19 (twice) as an `unrepresented` article beside `יוֹם` holding the whole adverbial, on the ground that *to* is the supplied function word rule 33 gives an adverbial accusative and no English word stands for the article (rule 29). The finished corpus instead fuses the pair as one `Td`+`Ncmsa` unit under rule 30 in eight units, headed on *day*. Both readings are defensible and the chapter is uniform; a later chapter meeting this string should weigh the corpus before choosing.

report: Read all 54 candidate groups and then the full dump end to end, since the table is keyed by source lemma and cannot show the chapter's five `added` units. One real cross-verse split found, in one verse.

Split: `נָכַר` hiphil with a bare object suffix, rendered *take knowledge of X*. RUT.2.10 gives the supplied *of* to the verb under rule 44; RUT.2.19 gave it to the suffix as a construct rectum under rule 19. The Hebrew writes a bare object suffix in both, MACULA tags both construct (Vhc, Vhrmsc), and the ASV wrote one idiom for both, so nothing in the source licenses the difference. Patched RUT.2.19 to rule 44, which also brings it into line with RUT.2.3 (`וַיִּקֶר` → *her hap was to light on the portion*), the chapter's third instance of an English verb reaching a bare Hebrew object through a supplied preposition.

Checked and found licensed, not splits: `הֲ` unrepresented at v.8 (*Hearest thou not*, inversion alone) beside *have* at v.9 (fronted auxiliary), rule 17; `אֲשֶׁר` with a resumptive suffix fused to *whose* at v.2 and v.12 but split at v.19's *with whom*, which is rule 22's two branches (possessive suffix on a noun vs suffix on a preposition the ASV renders separately); *and when* / *and how* / *And when* at v.9, v.11, v.15 as rule 55 pairs beside v.22's *and* plus a distributed second *that*, which rule 55's scope carve-out requires because one written `כִּי` governs both clauses; `בְּשָׂדֶה אַחֵר` at v.8 and v.22, where only v.22 writes *any* (rule 15); the partitives *some from* (v.16) and *one of* (v.20), both whole on the `מִן`; supplied object pronouns marked `added` uniformly at v.14, v.16 and v.18; verb-plus-particle kept with the verb in all eight places.

Left standing rather than patched, both recorded as conventions. RUT.2.23: rule 29's fronting sentence would give the single written *the* to the article on the innermost rectum of `כְּלוֹת קְצִיר־הַשְּׂעֹרִים`, but that *the* stands before *end*, two levels out, and the outer construct independently needs a supplied determiner; rule 29 does not settle a three-member chain with one written *the*, so the verse's reading stands and the competing one is named in the log. RUT.2.19 `הַיּוֹם` → *to day* twice: the chapter splits it (article `unrepresented`, `יוֹם` holding the whole adverbial under rules 29 and 33) where the corpus's eight `Td`+`Ncmsa` units fuse under rule 30. Both readings are defensible and the chapter is internally uniform, so I did not overwrite the accepted edges to match the corpus.

BSB disagreements: none is a genuine error. The Td (10), C (4), R (7) and Sn (4) classes are the documented convention difference, BSB attaching articles, conjunctions, prepositions and paragogic nuns to their host words where the ASV writes no English for them; every one of the ASV-side marks is licensed by rule 29, rule 14, rules 27/40 or rule 32. The singletons are each ruled: `זֶה` v.7 (the ASV writes no *this*, and the supplied *save that* answers to no morpheme, rule 55); `גַם` v.8 (the fused *neither* carries coordination and negation only, rule 30); `שֹׁל` v.16 (`גַּם` holds the one adverb written, rule 56); the resumptive `וֹ` v.19 (rule 22's two-word split); `הוּא` v.20 (resuming pronoun the ASV realizes once by the noun, rules 20, 22).

One amendment returned, to rule 19. Its suffix-rectum sentence ('the rectum may be a pronominal suffix rather than a noun, and nothing changes') reads as covering any *of + pronoun*, which is what RUT.2.19 reached for; the amendment marks the boundary against rule 44 in rule 19's own text rather than leaving the over-broad sentence in place. No new rules.
